vocabulary.definition: the main reason for something; a base or foundation
examples: The manager didn't have any basis for firing the employee.
On the basis of my ten years of loyalty to this company, I feel that I deserve three weeks vacation.

vocabulary.definition: to be conscious of; to be knowledgeable about
examples: The new staff member wasn't aware of the company's position on working a second job.
Are you aware of the new employee's past work history?

vocabulary.definition: n., an advantage provided to an employee in addition to salary; v., to take advantage of
examples: Although the analyst earned a better salary at his new job, his benefits were better at his previous job.
We all benefit from the company's policy of semiannual reviews.

vocabulary.definition: to pay; to make up for
examples: The company compensates employees for overtime by paying double for extra hours.
The company will compensate employees for any travel expenses.
Senior management is handling these contract negotiations delicately.
The manager delicately asked about the health of his client.

vocabulary.definition: able to participate in something; qualified
examples: Some employees may be eligible for the tuition reimbursement plan.
I don't understand why I'm not eligible if I have been with the company for over a year.

vocabulary.definition: with the ability to change; loosely
examples: My manager thinks flexibly, enabling herself to solve many sticky problems.
We need to respond flexibly if we want to keep customers in this competitive market.

vocabulary.definition: to talk for the purpose of reaching an agreement, especially on prices or contracts
examples: You must know what you want and what you can accept when you negotiate a salary.
The associate looked forward to the day that she would be able to negotiate her own contracts.

vocabulary.definition: n., an increase in salary; v., to move up
examples: With his raise, Mr. Drvoshanov was able to afford to buy a new car.
We need to raise the standard for timeliness.

vocabulary.definition: to stop working; to withdraw from a business or profession
examples: She retired at the age of 64 but continued to be very active with volunteer work.
Many people would like to win the lottery and retire.
The day that Ms. Weng became fully vested in the retirement plan, she gave her two weeks' notice.
The company has a vested interest in the happiness of its employees.

vocabulary.definition: the money paid for work done, usually hourly
examples: Hourly wages have increased by 20 percent over the last two years.
The intern spends more than half of her wages on rent.
